risks: Dual-patch double emission: both the http.ClientRequest.prototype patch AND the undici setGlobalDispatcher patch can fire for the same logical request when an SDK call routes through node:https.request indirectly (mitigation: the SDK tests assert entries.length === 1, not >= 1, so a double emission fails the assertion and surfaces the regression instead of silently emitting two entries).

SDK test gate-shape parity risk: the new *.sdk.integration.test.ts files must copy the horizon-7 raw-HTTPS gate shape verbatim (hasKey via length>0 check, if/else describe/describe.skip, two-setImmediate flush, JSON.stringify no-key safety, try/finally install/restore); any drift from this template (e.g. forgetting the second setImmediate tick, using truthy check that treats '' as set) reintroduces the horizon-7 gotchas into the SDK surface.

Jest 29 + Node 22 + testEnvironment: 'node' does not intercept globalThis.fetch: per discoveries.md horizon-9 entry 'jest-29-node-22-fetch-bridge-broken', Node's bootstrap lazy-loader spawns a fresh bundled undici for globalThis.fetch under Jest, so the dual-patch surface may not engage on the globalThis.fetch path; the SDK tests must therefore either (a) drive traffic through the SDK's own internal fetch which routes through the same globalDispatcher the patch wrapped, or (b) explicitly import undici and call ud.fetch when SDK-routed traffic does not engage — the rubric must lock one of these in advance to avoid a silently-skipped surface.

Dual-patch install/restore cross-test contamination: three new SDK suites plus the existing horizon-7 raw-HTTPS suites plus horizon-9's global-fetch-capture suite all share global http.ClientRequest.prototype and global undici dispatcher state; if any SDK suite forgets interceptor.restore() in a finally (or throws between install and restore), subsequent tests across the same jest run see a stale wrapper; mitigation: enforce try/finally install/restore discipline per the gate-shape parity risk above.

Ratifying the transport decision in decisions.md turns an implicit horizon-8 call into a written, dated constraint so the next horizon does not re-derive it. The decisions.md append is a one-line dated bullet (per the existing 14-entry format `- YYYY-MM-DD | horizon N | <summary> — because <rationale>`) folded into this phase as bookkeeping tied to the shim's existence.

rubric.label: Shim file exports createSdkFetchShim factory with correct signature
rubric.ruleStatement: The deliverable's primary surface must expose createSdkFetchShim with a signature of (input: RequestInfo | URL, init?: RequestInit) => Promise<Response>; this is the load-bearing shape criterion (c).10 means the factory is exported exactly once with that signature and is importable from the declared path with zero ceremony; 8 is a competent implementation that meets the signature and exports cleanly; minScore is the bar for ACCEPTABLE (the shape is real and resolvable).
passCriteria: packages/llm-http-proxy/src/sdk-fetch-shim.ts exists on disk and contains exactly one named export: createSdkFetchShim (no default export, no re-export from this module).

Importing createSdkFetchShim via `import { createSdkFetchShim } from './sdk-fetch-shim'` from the sibling file resolves to a function whose .length is 1 and whose declared return type is Promise<Response>.

The first parameter is annotated as RequestInfo | URL (or its `unknown`-shaped equivalent) and the optional second parameter is annotated as RequestInit (or includes body, method, headers in its declared shape).
failureExamples: The file exists but exports a default object containing the factory instead of a named export — every consumer that wrote `import { createSdkFetchShim } from ...` breaks even though `node -e "require('./sdk-fetch-shim')"` seems to work.

The factory is declared as `function createSdkFetchShim(): any` because the author assumed `any` would be loose enough to satisfy the SDK callers; consumers downstream then get Promise<any> and lose the Web Response contract silently at compile time.

The first parameter is typed `string` instead of `RequestInfo | URL`, so passing a Request object (which is what the SDK providers do in practice) fails tsc at the SDK call site even though `node:https.request` would have accepted it after the internal cast.

rubric.label: Return type satisfies every installed @ai-sdk/* provider FetchFunction
rubric.ruleStatement: The shim's return value must be typed (via satisfies clause or explicit cast) against the FetchFunction type of each installed @ai-sdk/{anthropic,openai,google} provider so that `tsc --noEmit` locks the contract against the real SDK type — not just any function. 10 means each provider's FetchFunction is referenced in the satisfies clause and a fresh typecheck fails if the shape drifts; 8 means the typecheck passes against the installed providers with no `any`/`unknown` escape hatches; minScore is the bar for ACCEPTABLE (the contract is locked, not trusted).
passCriteria: The file imports the FetchFunction (or its enclosing options type) from at least one of @ai-sdk/anthropic, @ai-sdk/openai, or @ai-sdk/google — visible as an import statement in the file.

The factory's return type uses a `satisfies ...FetchFunction` clause or a wrapping function whose declared return type is assignable to FetchFunction — grep for `satisfies` or a `: (input: ... => Promise<...>)` cast touching a FetchFunction reference.
Running `npm run typecheck` from packages/llm-http-proxy exits 0 with the new file present (no tsc errors mentioning FetchFunction, satisfies, or provider types).
No occurrence of `: any`, `as any`, or `// @ts-expect-error` inside sdk-fetch-shim.ts — the typecheck is doing the locking, not the author.
failureExamples: The author typed the return as `Promise<Response>` (which matches the web standard) but did not anchor it against any SDK FetchFunction — when @ai-sdk/google later bumps to a FetchFunction signature that drops a method overload, the shim compiles fine in isolation but fails inside the horizon-10 SDK integration test at the assignment site.

The author used a single `satisfies AnthropicFetchFunction` clause but `openai` and `google` ship subtly different signatures (e.g., openai's FetchFunction is `(input, init?) => Promise<Response>` with `input` as `string | URL | Request`); the openai suite then typechecks green via structural compat in this repo but breaks the moment the openai package tightens its FetchFunction generic.
The author cast the return value to `any` to silence a single tsc error about a missing method on the shim's response — the gate passes but every SDK provider downstream now has untyped errors.

rubric.label: Translation between Web Request/Response and node:https round-trips bytes correctly
rubric.ruleStatement: The shim must translate the SDK's Web Request shape into a node:https.request call that preserves method, headers (lowercased), and body (string | Buffer | undefined from init.body), and translate the IncomingMessage back into a Web Response carrying status, statusText, headers, and a ReadableStream body built from the buffered chunks. 10 means a round-trip test against a real local https server returns identical bytes and headers with a non-empty body; 8 means the code handles the documented cases (string body, headers, status) and a single representative round-trip works; minScore is the bar for ACCEPTABLE (no obvious byte or header loss on the happy path).
passCriteria: Header copy goes through a lowercasing step (e.g., a Headers object is constructed from the IncomingMessage's raw headers before being exposed on the Response) — visible as either `new Headers(...)` or an explicit `.toLowerCase()` pass in the file.

The IncomingMessage body is collected by listening for 'data' events until 'end' fires, then wrapped in a ReadableStream (not returned as a Node Readable, not returned as a string); grep for `on('data'`, `on('end'`, and `new ReadableStream` (or `Readable.from`).
The Response carries `status` (number from res.statusCode) and `statusText` (string from res.statusMessage) — both field names appear in the constructor call to `new Response(...)` or equivalent.
The body branches cover at least `string` and `undefined` in the init.body handling — `if (init?.body !== undefined)` or an explicit `typeof init.body === 'string'` check is visible.
failureExamples: The author forwards res.headers directly into the Response constructor without lowercasing, so a server that sets `Content-Type` shows up as `content-type` on the SDK side but a consumer that reads via `response.headers.get('Content-Type')` (the form the SDKs use) gets null — passes a quick `Object.keys(response.headers)` smoke test but fails any real SDK call.

The author returns the IncomingMessage wrapped in a Node Readable instead of a Web ReadableStream, so the SDK's `await response.text()` hangs forever (Node Readable is not a ReadableStream under the Web stream protocols); a manual `fetch(url)` works but the SDK stalls — the failure shows up only in horizon-10's SDK integration tests, not in this phase.

The author awaits `res.on('end', resolve)` but forgot to drain the body into a buffer before constructing the Response, so the stream is empty by the time `new Response(stream)` runs — passes typecheck and lint, returns `{ status: 200 }` with an empty body.

rubric.label: Shim is NOT re-exported from src/index.ts and is marked test-only at file scope
rubric.ruleStatement: The shim must remain a test-only surface — it must not appear in src/index.ts's export surface, and the file itself must carry a header comment asserting its test-only status (zero-hard-deps + no-new-exported-symbols invariant). 10 means src/index.ts is untouched, the header comment names the test-only purpose, and no other production source file imports from sdk-fetch-shim; 8 means the file is importable from test code and absent from the public API; minScore is the bar for ACCEPTABLE (the public API surface is unchanged and the file declares its scope).
passCriteria: `git diff src/index.ts` is empty after the phase — the public barrel file is byte-identical to its pre-phase state.

sdk-fetch-shim.ts opens with a comment block whose first non-comment line is not an export — the comment contains the word 'test-only' or equivalent ('not re-exported', 'internal test surface', 'not for production use').

`grep -R "sdk-fetch-shim" packages/llm-http-proxy/src --include="*.ts"` returns hits only inside test files (*.test.ts, *.integration.test.ts, *.sdk.integration.test.ts) — no production source imports the shim.
No new dependency is added to packages/llm-http-proxy/package.json (the shim uses only node:https and the @types/node fetch globals already pinned in devDependencies).

The author adds a runtime dependency (e.g., `node-fetch`, `undici`) to packages/llm-http-proxy/package.json because `node:https.request` had a typing gap they didn't want to wrestle with — this violates the zero-hard-deps invariant and silently enlarges the install surface for every downstream consumer.

phases.name: Add Anthropic SDK integration test

rubric.ruleStatement: Each test must capture the live undici global dispatcher before Interceptor.install() runs and assert equality after restore in afterEach so an un-restored install (a real dual-patch leak) fails the suite instead of poisoning the next *.integration.test.ts. 10 = originalDispatcher captured in beforeEach, afterEach asserts `expect(ud.getGlobalDispatcher()).toBe(originalDispatcher)` AFTER interceptor.restore(), and the test body wraps install/generateText/asserts in try { ... } finally { interceptor.restore(); }; 8 = all three pieces present with cosmetic differences; minScore 7 = interceptor.restore() is reachable on both the success and throw paths of the test body.

failureExamples: Developer only puts `interceptor.restore()` in the test body's finally and skips the afterEach assertion — if the body throws before reaching finally (e.g. a typo in the SDK call), no assertion fires and the next *.integration.test.ts inherits a poisoned global dispatcher

passCriteria: Exactly two `await new Promise(r => setImmediate(r))` calls are awaited in sequence before the assertions (not one, not three)
Assertion is `expect(entries.length).toBe(1)` with literal 1, NOT `toBeGreaterThan(0)` / `toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1)` / `>= 1`

Developer awaits only one `setImmediate` — the WrappingDispatcher's onComplete resolves in a later microtask, entries.length reads 0, and the suite fails with the wrong symptom (zero capture) instead of the correct one (double capture or shim leak)

Developer asserts `entries[0].model` is truthy but skips the 'claude' substring check — a captured entry from a different suite that leaked in (because dual-patch restoration is broken) would still pass

rubric.label: Horizon-7 gate shape used verbatim
rubric.ruleStatement: The file must use the horizon-7 raw-HTTPS gate shape verbatim — length>0 guard on `GEMINI_API_KEY ?? GOOGLE_API_KEY`, top-level `if (hasKey) describe(...) else describe.skip(...)`, two `setImmediate` flushes, and try/finally install/restore. 10 = structurally identical to horizon-7's gate with every element present and in order; 8 = competent implementation with all five elements functionally equivalent; minScore=7 means the gate must actually skip-vs-run on the env var AND try/finally must restore so a thrown assertion does not leak the swapped dispatcher into later suites.
passCriteria: File path is exactly `packages/llm-http-proxy/src/gemini.sdk.integration.test.ts` (matches the `*.sdk.integration.test.ts` discovery pattern).

File contains `const apiKey = process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY ?? process.env.GOOGLE_API_KEY;` and a `hasKey` boolean derived from `apiKey !== undefined && apiKey.length > 0` (length>0 guard, not truthiness).

Top-level structure is `if (hasKey) describe(...) else describe.skip('gemini SDK suite (skip: GEMINI_API_KEY unset)', placeholderFn)` — the `describe.skip` lives at the top level, not nested inside a `describe` body.
Between the `await generateText(...)` resolution and the `entries.length === 1` assertion there are exactly two consecutive `await new Promise(r => setImmediate(r))` calls.
`new Interceptor({...}).install()` is wrapped in a `try { ... } finally { interceptor.restore(); }` block so a failed assertion cannot leave the global undici dispatcher swapped.
failureExamples: Using `if (apiKey)` truthiness check instead of `hasKey` length>0 — an empty-string `GEMINI_API_KEY=""` makes the suite attempt the real network call and fail instead of skipping cleanly.

Placing the skip inside `describe('gemini SDK suite', () => { if (!hasKey) { it.skip(...); return; } ... })` — Jest still loads and evaluates the file's top-level imports (which may touch undici's global dispatcher) even when the suite is meant to skip.
Using a single `setImmediate` flush — on Jest 29 + Node 22 the dual-patch's log emit can settle on the next macrotask, so the entries.length === 1 assertion races and flakes on slow CI.

Omitting try/finally — if `generateText` throws (e.g., DNS failure on a sandbox runner), `interceptor.restore()` never runs and the global undici dispatcher stays swapped, poisoning the horizon-9 global-fetch suite that runs after.

rubric.label: No per-file fetch shim override passed to the SDK provider
rubric.ruleStatement: The `createGoogle({...})` call must NOT be passed a per-file `fetch:` override — the horizon-9 dual-patch (http.ClientRequest.prototype wrap + undici setGlobalDispatcher) must be the sole interception surface for SDK traffic in this file. 10 = grep proves zero shim references in non-comment code AND `createGoogle({...})` has no `fetch:` key; 8 = no shim passed and only an in-comment mention remains; minScore=9 because passing any shim makes the test invalid as a dual-patch verification — even one runtime reference drops the score below acceptable.
passCriteria: `grep -nE 'createSdkFetchShim|createNodeHttpsFetch' packages/llm-http-proxy/src/gemini.sdk.integration.test.ts` returns no lines outside comment blocks.
The `createGoogle({...})` options object, inspected at the call site, contains no `fetch:` property.
The only interception setup in the file is `new Interceptor({...}).install()` (with optional try/require undici for `setGlobalDispatcher` round-tripping) — no other interception surface is engaged.
failureExamples: Developer adds `fetch: createSdkFetchShim()` to `createGoogle({...})` because horizon-7's gate used raw HTTPS — the SDK now routes around the dual-patch entirely, so the test passes even if the horizon-9 dual-patch is broken; the suite verifies nothing about the interception surface it claims to.

Developer imports `createNodeHttpsFetch` into the gemini test "for consistency with horizon-7" — the import itself signals intent to a reviewer who greps for shims and may be "fixed" by a future contributor into a real call.

Developer passes `fetch: globalThis.fetch` "to be explicit" — same bypass; the dual-patch never sees the request, and `entries.length === 1` will only pass if the SDK silently swallowed an unrelated error.

rubric.label: Dual-patch capture asserted with correct LlmLogEntry shape
rubric.ruleStatement: The suite must assert that the dual-patch actually captured the SDK-issued request — `entries.length === 1` plus the LlmLogEntry fields the default parser populates (model containing `gemini`, url containing the expected Gemini endpoint fragment, non-negative inputTokens/outputTokens). 10 = every relevant field asserted AND token-count uses `>= 0` (never `> 0`) to match the default parser's `usageMetadata`-blind behavior; 8 = `entries.length === 1` plus model/url asserted with `>= 0` tokens; minScore=7 means `entries.length === 1` must be present and at least one LlmLogEntry field beyond that must be asserted.
passCriteria: `expect(entries.length).toBe(1)` is present and uses `toBe`, not `toBeGreaterThan` (catches the dual-patch double-emit regression).
`expect(entries[0].model).toContain('gemini')` is present (or the equivalent substring of the actual model id).
`expect(entries[0].url).toContain(<expected Gemini URL fragment>)` is present — fragment derived from `GEMINI_BASE_URL` or `generativelanguage.googleapis.com`.
`expect(entries[0].inputTokens).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0)` AND `expect(entries[0].outputTokens).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0)` are present — NOT `.toBeGreaterThan(0)`.
failureExamples: Using `.toBeGreaterThan(0)` for tokens — the default parser in src/provider-parser.ts lines 86-102 only inspects `usage.completion_tokens` / `usage.output_tokens`, never `usageMetadata.promptTokenCount/candidatesTokenCount/totalTokenCount` (Gemini's camelCase response shape), so when the Gemini response carries only `usageMetadata` the parser returns 0 and the assertion fails spuriously with a real key set.

Asserting `expect(entries.length).toBeGreaterThan(0)` — does not detect the one-request-two-emits bug the dual-patch was built to prevent (one entry per interception surface); a double-emit regression would still pass.
Skipping the `url` assertion — the dual-patch could be capturing a request to the wrong host (e.g., a stale base URL) and `entries.length === 1` would still pass.
Asserting only `expect(entries[0]).toBeDefined()` — passes trivially even if every field is undefined.

rubric.label: API key leak guard present and correct
rubric.ruleStatement: The suite must guard against the captured API key appearing in any field of the LlmLogEntry via a `JSON.stringify(entries[0])` substring assertion that fails if the key value is present. 10 = guard uses the live env var value (or a guaranteed-impossible sentinel when the gate skipped), runs inside the executed branch only, and is positioned before `interceptor.restore()`; 8 = competent guard using the runtime key value; minScore=8 because a missing or wrong-target guard is a security regression even if the rest of the suite passes.
passCriteria: File contains an assertion of the form `expect(JSON.stringify(entries[0])).not.toContain(<key-source>)` where `<key-source>` is `apiKey` itself (resolved after the length>0 check), not a constant string like `'Bearer'` or the model id.
The guard runs inside the executed (`if (hasKey)`) branch — i.e., it is not inside the `describe.skip` block where it would never fire.
The guard executes after `generateText` resolves and before the `try` block's `finally` restores the interceptor, so a leaked key fails the suite loudly instead of being logged after teardown.
failureExamples: Omitting the guard entirely — the SDK may echo the API key in a masked request body or response header, and the suite silently passes with the secret embedded in test logs that get committed to CI artifacts and scraped by log aggregators.

Asserting `not.toContain('Bearer')` instead of `not.toContain(apiKey)` — `'Bearer'` is a constant substring that appears in any auth header, so the guard always passes and proves nothing about key leakage.
Putting the guard inside the `describe.skip` branch — when the suite actually runs with a real key, the guard is skipped too and provides zero protection.
Asserting against the model id or URL fragment instead of the key — fails for the wrong reason (model id never leaks); key still leaks silently into the captured entry.
